title: Reporting What People Said
overview: Put two past events in the right order, and report a conversation so the tenses still work a week later. Choose a reporting verb that matches the authority behind it. Say whether you did something or only meant to. Then check a written record against what was actually said.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: a dispute over minutes, a language guide and a witness statement.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Tell a past story and make clear which event came first
Report a conversation from last week with the tenses right
Report what somebody wanted done, without inventing authority
Say whether you did something or only meant to
Read a contract without being stopped by its formal phrases
Check a written record against what was actually said
Give a statement about an incident, in order
lectureScript:
This unit finishes something Unit 7 started, and it begins with a form you have never met.

The past perfect. Had, plus the past participle.
Nothing in Levels 1 or 2 teaches it, and nothing in this level has needed it until now.
It does one job. When you are already telling a story in the past, it marks the thing that happened BEFORE that.
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
Arrived is the main story. Had started is earlier still.
Listen to what happens if you take the had out.
When I arrived, the meeting started.
That now says the meeting waited for me and began once I was in the room. A completely different claim, and one word did it.
One warning, because learners overuse this once they meet it.
You do not need it when the order is already obvious. I got up, had breakfast and left is three past simples and it is perfect English.
Save the past perfect for the event that is genuinely out of order.

Now the second card, which is why the first one had to come first.
In Unit 7 you learned how to report a question, and how to choose a reporting verb. That unit stopped short of the tense on purpose.
Here is the rule. If your reporting verb is in the past, everything inside steps back one.
A present becomes a past. I work here becomes he said he worked there.
A past becomes a past perfect. I finished it becomes she said she had finished it.
Will becomes would. Can becomes could.
And the time words move as well, which Level 2 already taught you. Yesterday becomes the day before. Tomorrow becomes the next day. Here becomes there.
Two things about this are worth more than the rule itself.
The first is where it stops. The past perfect has nowhere further to go.
If somebody said I had already left, you report it unchanged. There is no had had finished.
The second is that you do not always have to do it.
If the thing is still true and you want your reader to know that, leave it in the present.
She said the office IS on the first floor tells the reader it still is.
She said the office WAS on the first floor leaves them wondering whether it has moved.
In a record, that is information, so make the choice on purpose.

The third card widens something Unit 7 gave you narrowly.
You had told and asked. In a written record those are often too blunt.
Invited. Advised. Urged. Requested. Instructed. Ordered. Forbade.
They run from an easily refused offer up to authority that cannot be refused, and choosing one is choosing what you say happened.
Almost all of them take the same shape: verb, person, to, plain verb. She advised us to wait.
Two break it, and they are the two everybody gets wrong.
Suggest never takes a person and to. She suggested waiting, or she suggested that I wait. Never she suggested me to wait.
And deny takes -ing. He denied sending it. Never he denied to send it.

The fourth card is about five verbs where both forms are possible and the meaning changes completely.
Level 2 gave you one of them: stopped to eat, against stopped eating.
Here are four more, and they matter because the two versions describe different facts.
I remember locking it means I locked it and I can recall doing so.
I remembered to lock it means I nearly forgot, and then I did it.
I forgot locking it means it was locked and I cannot recall it.
I forgot to lock it means the door is open.
In a report about a break-in those last two are not interchangeable in any way at all.
The pattern underneath all five is short. The -ing form is what happened. The to form is what was intended.

The last card is for reading more than for writing.
In accordance with. With regard to. In the event of. Subject to. On behalf of. Pending. With a view to.
These fill notices, contracts and minutes, and you need to be able to read them long before you need to write them.
One of them has a trap. With a view to takes an -ing form, because the to in it is a preposition and not an infinitive marker.
We met with a view to agreeing a timescale. Not to agree.
And a warning about all of them. They are heavy. Using them in a short email makes you sound stiff rather than professional.

The reading is about minutes that recorded something the meeting had not agreed.
Nobody lied. Somebody paraphrased, and lost a condition. And somewhere else a neutral verb became a loaded one.
Both of those are small. Together they produced a document that was wrong, and by the time anybody noticed it had gone to the client.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: To say something clearly and definitely.
words.example: She stated that the work had been completed.
practice: State is neutral: it takes no position on whether it is true.
It takes that plus a clause.
Its noun is statement.
State is the standard verb for minutes and records.
words.tutor: Report something neutrally with state. Ask the tutor whether any judgement crept in.

words.meaning: To say something briefly, in passing.
words.example: He mentioned that the seal had been replaced.
practice: Mention suggests it was not the main point.
It takes that plus a clause, or a direct object.
Mention never takes to before a person: mention it to her.
Its noun is mention, unchanged.
words.tutor: Report something said in passing. Ask the tutor whether mention suited its weight.

words.meaning: To give an account of something officially.
words.example: She reported that two boxes were missing.
practice: Report takes that, or a direct object.
You report something TO somebody.
Its noun is report.
Reported speech takes its name from this verb.
words.tutor: Report something officially. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: To observe something and record it.
words.example: The inspector noted that the gate was unlocked.
practice: Note is common in reports and minutes.
It carries a slight sense of putting it on record.
It takes that plus a clause.
Its noun is a note.
words.tutor: Report an observation with note. Ask the tutor how note differs from say.

words.meaning: To say something further, after what has already been said.
words.example: She added that the cost would be met locally.
practice: Add always follows something else: it cannot open an account.
It takes that plus a clause.
Add is neutral and very common in minutes.
In addition is the connective from the same root.
words.tutor: Add a second point in reported speech. Ask the tutor whether it followed something.

words.meaning: To make a remark, often a considered one.
words.example: He observed that nobody had signed the form.
practice: Observe as a reporting verb is formal and slightly weighty.
It also means to watch, and to follow a rule.
It takes that plus a clause.
Its noun here is observation.
words.tutor: Report a considered remark. Ask the tutor whether observe was too formal.

groups.title: Reporting verbs that carry a judgement

words.meaning: To say that something is not true.
words.example: He denied sending the second invoice.
practice: Deny takes an -ing form, or that plus a clause.
Never deny TO do something.
Its noun is denial.
Denying is not the same as disproving.
words.tutor: Report a denial. Ask the tutor to check the form after deny.

words.meaning: To say you are unhappy about something.
words.example: She complained that nobody had replied.
practice: Complain takes about a thing, and to a person.
It takes that plus a clause when you report what was said.
Its noun is complaint.
Reporting somebody as complaining is not neutral.
words.tutor: Report a complaint. Ask the tutor whether complained was fair.

words.meaning: To speak with too much pride about what you have done.
words.example: He boasted that he had finished in half the time.
practice: Boast takes about, or that plus a clause.
It is strongly negative: it accuses the speaker of vanity.
Never use it in minutes unless you can defend it.
Its noun is a boast.
words.tutor: Report a boast. Ask the tutor whether you could defend the word.

words.meaning: To advise somebody strongly and repeatedly.
words.example: She urged us to get it in writing.
practice: Urge takes a person plus to plus a plain verb.
It is stronger than advise and weaker than order.
Its noun is an urge, though that means something different.
Urging carries no authority, only insistence.
words.tutor: Report strong advice. Ask the tutor to check the form after urge.

words.meaning: To say something that removes somebody's worry.
words.example: He reassured us that the parts were on the way.
practice: Reassure takes a person plus that plus a clause.
It implies there was a worry to remove.
Its noun is reassurance.
Reassuring somebody wrongly is worse than saying nothing.
words.tutor: Report a reassurance. Ask the tutor whether there was a worry to remove.

words.meaning: To admit something you would rather not.
words.example: She confessed that she had not read it.
practice: Confess takes that, or to plus an -ing form.
It is stronger than admit and carries more weight.
Its noun is confession.
Use it only where the admission genuinely cost the speaker.
words.tutor: Report a confession. Ask the tutor whether confess or admit was right.

words.meaning: To tell somebody to do something, with authority.
words.example: The inspector ordered the line to be stopped.
practice: Order takes a person plus to plus a plain verb.
It claims real authority: use it only where there was some.
Its noun is an order.
Ordering is the strongest of this group.
words.tutor: Report an order. Ask the tutor whether the speaker really had authority.

words.meaning: To tell somebody officially how to do something.
words.example: We were instructed to keep a written record.
practice: Instruct takes a person plus to plus a plain verb.
It is formal and slightly softer than order.
Its noun is an instruction.
Instructions are usually written; orders are often spoken.
words.tutor: Report an instruction. Ask the tutor how instruct differs from order.

words.meaning: To ask for something formally.
words.example: She requested a copy of the report.
practice: Request takes a thing, or that plus a clause.
Request somebody TO do something is possible but stiff.
Its noun is a request.
A request can be refused; an order cannot.
words.tutor: Report a formal request. Ask the tutor whether it could have been refused.

words.meaning: To tell somebody what you think they should do.
words.example: He advised us to wait for the certificate.
practice: Advise takes a person plus to plus a plain verb.
Advise is the verb, with an s; advice is the noun, with a c.
That spelling pair is worth learning as a pair.
Advice is uncountable: a piece of advice.
words.tutor: Report advice. Ask the tutor to check advise and advice.

words.meaning: To order somebody not to do something.
words.example: The notice forbids parking on the verge.
practice: Forbid takes a person plus to plus a plain verb.
Its past forms are forbade and forbidden.
Forbidden is much commoner than the verb itself.
Forbid is the opposite of permit.
words.tutor: Report a prohibition. Ask the tutor to check the past forms.

words.meaning: To allow something, officially.
words.example: Visitors are not permitted beyond this point.
practice: Permit takes a person plus to plus a plain verb.
It doubles its t: permitted, permitting.
Its noun is a permit, stressed on the first part.
Permit is the formal allow.
words.tutor: Write a rule with permit. Ask the tutor to check the doubled t.

words.meaning: To repeat somebody's exact words.
words.example: She quoted the clause in full.
practice: Quoting means the exact words, inside quotation marks.
Quote takes from for the source.
Its noun is a quotation, or informally a quote.
If you change a word, you are no longer quoting.
words.tutor: Quote something exactly. Ask the tutor whether every word was the same.

words.meaning: To give the meaning in your own words.
words.example: I have paraphrased his reply rather than quoting it.
practice: Paraphrasing keeps the meaning and changes the words.
It is honest as long as you say that is what you did.
It is both a verb and a noun.
A paraphrase can be shorter; it must not be different.
words.tutor: Paraphrase something. Ask the tutor whether the meaning survived.

words.meaning: In exactly the words that were used.
words.example: The minutes record her reply verbatim.
practice: Verbatim means word for word.
It is both an adverb and an adjective: a verbatim record.
It is formal and comes from Latin.
A verbatim record is not the same as an accurate one.
words.tutor: Say what is recorded verbatim. Ask the tutor whether verbatim guarantees accuracy.

words.meaning: The general meaning, without the detail.
words.example: I only caught the gist of what she said.
practice: The gist is the main point, not the words.
It is almost always used with of.
Getting the gist is enough for some purposes and not others.
It is pronounced with a soft g, like jist.
words.tutor: Say what you caught the gist of. Ask the tutor when the gist is not enough.

words.meaning: To repeat somebody's words wrongly.
words.example: He claims he was misquoted in the summary.
practice: Mis- plus quote: to quote wrongly.
Misquoting can be accidental or deliberate.
Its noun is a misquotation.
Being misquoted is a common complaint about minutes.
words.tutor: Report a misquotation. Ask the tutor whether it looked accidental.

words.meaning: To say who said or did something.
words.example: The remark was attributed to the chair.
practice: Attribute takes to.
The stress moves: a-TRIB-ute for the verb, AT-tri-bute for the noun.
Attributing a remark wrongly is a serious error in minutes.
Unattributed means nobody is named.
words.tutor: Attribute a remark. Ask the tutor to check where you put the stress.

words.meaning: Where information came from.
words.example: The report does not name its source.
practice: A source can be a person or a document.
Source takes of, or for.
An unnamed source cannot be checked.
It is also a verb: to source materials.
words.starter: The … does not name its source for …
words.tutor: Say what has no named source. Ask the tutor why that matters.

words.meaning: A person who saw something happen.
words.example: Two witnesses gave the same account.
practice: A witness saw it; a source may only have been told.
It is also a verb: to witness an accident.
To witness a signature is a separate legal meaning.
Its plural is witnesses.
words.tutor: Report what a witness said. Ask the tutor how a witness differs from a source.

words.meaning: A person who speaks officially for an organisation.
words.example: A spokesperson said the matter was under review.
practice: A spokesperson speaks for others, not for themselves.
Spokesperson is the neutral form of spokesman.
Its plural is spokespeople.
What a spokesperson says is the organisation's position.
words.tutor: Report a spokesperson. Ask the tutor whose view was being given.

words.meaning: Something said or written officially, on the record.
words.example: They issued a statement the same afternoon.
practice: A statement is prepared; a remark is not.
You issue, release or make a statement.
It comes from state.
A written statement can be quoted verbatim.
words.starter: They issued a statement saying that …
words.tutor: Report a statement. Ask the tutor how it differs from a remark.

words.meaning: A claim that somebody has done something wrong, not yet proved.
words.example: The allegation has not been investigated.
practice: An allegation is unproved by definition.
It takes of, or that plus a clause.
Its verb is allege, and its adverb allegedly.
Calling something an allegation is not calling it false.
words.tutor: Report an allegation. Ask the tutor whether allegation implied it was false.

grammar.title: It had already gone: the tense for the earlier of two past events
grammar.explanation:
This form is new. Nothing in Levels 1 or 2 teaches it, and nothing in this
level so far has needed it.
It does one job, and the job is simple: when you are already telling a story
in the past, it marks the thing that happened BEFORE that.
grammar.rule:
had + the past participle. It never changes for the person.
I had, you had, she had, they had. Always had.

Two past events, and one came first:
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
  arrived     = past simple, the main story
  had started = past perfect, earlier still

By the time we rang, they had closed.
She could not sign it because she had left her glasses at home.

You do NOT need it when the order is already obvious:
I got up, had breakfast and left.  (all simple, and correct)

Time words that go with it:
already, just, never, by the time, before, until then

Compare the two. The difference is real:
When I arrived, the meeting started.     (I came, THEN it began)
When I arrived, the meeting had started. (it began, THEN I came)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these: The meeting started at nine. I arrived at half past.
1. Which came first? The meeting starting.
2. Which is the main story? My arriving — that is what I am telling you about.
3. The main story takes the past simple: when I arrived.
4. The earlier event takes the past perfect: had started.
Answer: When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
Without had, the sentence would say the meeting waited for me.
grammar.mistake:
Using it for a plain sequence makes writing heavy for no gain.
Heavy: I had got up, had had breakfast and had left.
Better: I got up, had breakfast and left.
Save it for the event that is genuinely out of order.
grammar.tip: One story in the past simple. The thing that happened before it takes had.
grammar.practice:
Choose the past simple or the past perfect.
1. When I ___ (arrive), the meeting ___ (already start).
2. By the time we ___ (ring), they ___ (close).
3. She ___ (not sign) it because she ___ (leave) her glasses at home.
4. I ___ (get) up, ___ (have) breakfast and ___ (leave).
5. The parts ___ (be) ordered before anybody ___ (check) the stock.
Now say what each of these means.
6. When I arrived, the meeting started.
7. When I arrived, the meeting had started.
grammar.answers:
1. arrived / had already started  2. rang / had closed
3. did not sign / had left  4. got / had / left (a plain sequence, no perfect needed)
5. had been ordered / checked
6. I arrived first, and then it began.
7. It began first, and I came in late.
Numbers 6 and 7 are the whole card: one word changes who was waiting for whom.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: He said he had finished: what happens to the tense when you report it
grammar.explanation:
Unit 7 taught you the word order of a reported question and the choice of
reporting verb. It stopped short of the tense, on purpose, because the tense
needs the form on the card before this one.
Here it is: when the reporting verb is in the past, everything steps back.
grammar.rule:
THE BACKSHIFT, one step each:
present simple  -> past simple      I work   -> he said he WORKED
present cont.   -> past continuous  I am working -> he WAS WORKING
past simple     -> past perfect     I finished -> he HAD FINISHED
present perfect -> past perfect     I have sent -> he HAD SENT
will -> would     can -> could

The past perfect does not step back again. It has nowhere to go.
'I had finished' -> he said he had finished.

OTHER WORDS MOVE TOO, which Level 2 taught you:
here -> there    now -> then    this -> that
yesterday -> the day before    tomorrow -> the next day

WHEN YOU DO NOT BACKSHIFT:
if the reporting verb is present: he SAYS he works here
if it is still true and you want to say so:
  She said the office IS on the first floor.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Report this, a week later: 'I finished it yesterday,' she said.
1. The reporting verb is past: she said.
2. So everything steps back one.
3. finished is a past simple, and one step back from that is the past perfect: had finished.
4. yesterday moves too: the day before.
Answer: She said she had finished it the day before.
If you leave yesterday in, a reader a week later will take it to mean yesterday.
grammar.mistake:
The past perfect cannot step back twice, and learners try.
No: He said he had had finished.
Yes: He said he had finished.
Once you reach the past perfect, the backshift has run out of room.
grammar.tip: One step back for each tense. The past perfect is the end of the road.
grammar.practice:
Report each one, a week later.
1. 'I work here,' he said.
2. 'I am working on it now,' she said.
3. 'I finished it yesterday,' she said.
4. 'I have already sent it,' he said.
5. 'I will ring you tomorrow,' she said.
6. 'I can come on Friday,' he said.
7. 'I had already left,' she said.
Now decide whether to backshift.
8. 'The office is on the first floor,' she said. (it still is, and you want to say so)
grammar.answers:
1. He said he worked there.
2. She said she was working on it then.
3. She said she had finished it the day before.
4. He said he had already sent it.
5. She said she would ring me the next day.
6. He said he could come on Friday.
7. She said she had already left. (no further back to go)
8. She said the office is on the first floor. (still true, so you may leave it)
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Ordered, urged, advised, permitted: reporting what somebody wanted done
grammar.explanation:
Unit 7 gave you told and asked, and the test of who had the power.
This card widens the set, because in a written record told and asked are
often too blunt. Each of these verbs carries a different amount of force,
and choosing one is choosing what you are saying happened.
grammar.rule:
All of these take the SAME shape:
verb + person + TO + plain verb
She advised us to wait.  He urged them to reconsider.
The negative puts NOT before the to: she advised us NOT to sign.

Ordered by force, weakest first:
invited    an offer, easily refused
advised    an opinion about what is best
urged      strong and repeated, but no authority
requested  formal, and still refusable
instructed official, expected to be followed
ordered    authority, and not refusable
forbade    authority, in the negative

Two break the shape and must be learned separately:
suggest -> She suggested WAITING, or THAT WE WAIT.
           NEVER: she suggested us to wait.
deny    -> He denied SENDING it.
           NEVER: he denied to send it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Report this: your colleague, who has no authority over you, says twice
'You really should get that in writing.'
1. Did they have authority? No, so ordered and instructed are out.
2. Was it stronger than a single piece of advice? Yes, they said it twice.
3. Strong, repeated, no authority: that is urged.
Answer: She urged me to get it in writing.
Advised would be true but would lose the insistence. Told would invent authority.
grammar.mistake:
suggest is the one everybody gets wrong, because every verb beside it fits the shape.
No: She suggested me to wait.
Yes: She suggested waiting. Or: She suggested that I wait.
Same for recommend: he recommended waiting, not he recommended me to wait.
grammar.tip: Most take person + to + verb. suggest and deny do not. Learn those two as exceptions.
grammar.practice:
Report each one with the verb that fits.
1. Your manager, with authority: 'Stop the line.'
2. A colleague, twice, with no authority: 'Get it in writing.'
3. An inspector, officially: 'Keep a written record.'
4. A friend: 'I think you should wait.'
5. A notice: 'No parking on the verge.'
6. A colleague: 'Why not wait until Friday?'
7. He said he had not sent the second invoice.
Now correct these.
8. She suggested me to wait.
9. He denied to send it.
grammar.answers:
1. My manager ordered me to stop the line.
2. A colleague urged me to get it in writing.
3. The inspector instructed us to keep a written record.
4. A friend advised me to wait.
5. The notice forbids parking on the verge.
6. A colleague suggested waiting until Friday.
7. He denied sending the second invoice.
8. She suggested waiting. (or: that I wait)  9. He denied sending it.
7 or more right: good.

grammar.title: I remember locking it, or I remembered to lock it
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 showed you one verb where both forms are possible and the meaning
changes: stopped to eat, against stopped eating.
There are four more, and each of them matters in a written account, because
the two versions describe genuinely different events.
grammar.rule:
REMEMBER
I remember locking it.     = I locked it, and I can recall doing so.
I remembered to lock it.   = I did not forget. The memory came first.
-ing looks BACK. to looks FORWARD.

FORGET
I forgot locking it.       = I did lock it, but I cannot recall it.
I forgot to lock it.       = I did not lock it at all.
These describe opposite facts about the door.

REGRET
I regret telling him.      = I told him, and I wish I had not.
I regret to tell you ...   = I am about to give you bad news.

TRY
I tried moving it.         = I moved it, as an experiment.
I tried to move it.        = I attempted it, and probably failed.

STOP, which you have:
I stopped eating.          = I no longer eat.
I stopped to eat.          = I halted in order to eat.

The pattern under all five: -ing is the real event; to is the intention.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Which is true if the door is unlocked: I forgot locking it, or I forgot to lock it?
1. -ing looks back at a real event. I forgot locking it means it WAS locked.
2. to looks forward at an intention. I forgot to lock it means it was NOT.
3. The door is unlocked, so the locking never happened.
Answer: I forgot to lock it.
In a report about a break-in, those two sentences are not interchangeable.
grammar.mistake:
Learners choose by which sounds better, and the two are equally natural.
Ask instead: did it happen, or was it only intended?
I remember posting it  = it was posted.
I remembered to post it = it was posted, and I nearly forgot.
I forgot to post it    = it was NOT posted.
grammar.tip: -ing is what happened. to is what was meant to happen.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right form, and say what the sentence claims.
1. The door is unlocked. I forgot (locking / to lock) it.
2. I can picture myself doing it. I remember (locking / to lock) it.
3. I nearly forgot, but I did it. I remembered (locking / to lock) it.
4. I told him and I wish I had not. I regret (telling / to tell) him.
5. Bad news is coming. I regret (informing / to inform) you that ...
6. I moved it as an experiment. I tried (moving / to move) it.
7. I attempted it and failed. I tried (moving / to move) it.
8. I no longer eat there. I stopped (eating / to eat) there.
grammar.answers:
1. to lock (it never happened)  2. locking (it happened)
3. to lock (the memory came first)  4. telling (it happened)
5. to inform (bad news coming)  6. moving (it happened)
7. to move (only attempted)  8. eating (the habit ended)
6 and 7 are the same words describing opposite outcomes.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: In accordance with, with regard to: the formal preposition phrase
grammar.explanation:
Unit 2 gave you in charge of, under pressure, at risk: short phrases where
the preposition carried a meaning.
This set is longer, heavier and belongs to official writing. You will meet
these constantly in notices, contracts and minutes, and you need to be able
to read them before you need to write them.
grammar.rule:
in accordance with = following the rules of
  Work was carried out in accordance with the specification.
with regard to     = about, concerning
in the event of    = if this happens
  In the event of a failure, the alarm sounds.
subject to         = only if this is satisfied
  Approval is subject to a final inspection.
on behalf of       = as the representative of
with a view to     = in order eventually to. Takes -ING.
  We met with a view to agreeing a timescale.
prior to           = before
pending            = until a decision is made
  The post is suspended pending the investigation.

Two warnings. These are HEAVY. In speech, or in a short email, they make
you sound stiff rather than professional.
And with a view to takes -ing, because that to is a preposition.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Fill the gap: We met ___ ___ ___ ___ agreeing a timescale.
1. What does the sentence mean? We met in order eventually to agree one.
2. That is with a view to.
3. The to in that phrase is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing.
4. agreeing, not agree.
Answer: We met with a view to agreeing a timescale.
with a view to agree is the standard error, and it is very common.
grammar.mistake:
The heaviest error is using these where they are not wanted.
Stiff: With regard to your email, I am in receipt of the same.
Better: Thanks for your email.
Learn them to READ official writing. Write them only when the document is official.
grammar.tip: Learn these to read a contract. Use them only where a contract would.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing phrase.
1. Work was carried out ___ the specification. (following its rules)
2. ___ your letter of the 3rd, I can confirm the date. (about)
3. ___ a power failure, the alarm sounds. (if this happens)
4. Approval is ___ a final inspection. (only if satisfied)
5. I am writing ___ the residents. (as their representative)
6. We met ___ ___ agreeing a timescale. (in order eventually to)
7. The post is suspended ___ the investigation. (until it is decided)
Now correct these.
8. We met with a view to agree a timescale.
9. With regard to your email, I am in receipt of the same. (make it human)
grammar.answers:
1. in accordance with  2. With regard to  3. In the event of
4. subject to  5. on behalf of  6. with a view to  7. pending
8. with a view to agreeING (the to there is a preposition)
9. Thanks for your email. (the original is correct English and nobody talks like that)
7 or more right: good.

readings.title: What the Minutes Said I Said
readings.setting: An office, a fortnight after a meeting
readings.passage:
I asked for the minutes to be corrected and I was told I was being difficult.
What I had actually said was that I could not confirm the date until the survey came back.
What the minutes said was that I had refused to confirm the date.
Those are not the same thing, and by the time I saw them the paper had already gone to the client.
The person who wrote them had not misheard me. They had paraphrased, which is allowed, and lost the condition, which is not.
Every sentence I objected to had the same shape. A neutral verb replaced by a loaded one, or a condition quietly dropped.
He mentioned the delay became he complained about the delay.
She said she would look into it became she reassured us that it was in hand.
Nobody had lied. Each change was small, and the paper as a whole said something the meeting had not agreed.
I now do one thing that has saved me twice.
If a decision depends on a condition, I ask for my own words to be recorded verbatim, and I say so in the room.
It sounds fussy. It takes about eight seconds.
It is the only thing I have found that survives paraphrase.

readings.title: One Step Back, and No Further
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passage:
When you report what somebody said, and your reporting verb is in the past, the tenses inside step back one.
A present becomes a past. I work here becomes he said he worked there.
A past becomes a past perfect. I finished it becomes she said she had finished it.
Will becomes would, and can becomes could.
The rule is regular and learners pick it up quickly. Two things about it are less often explained.
The first is where the backshift stops. The past perfect has nowhere further to go.
If somebody said I had already left, you report it as she said she had already left, unchanged.
There is no such thing as had had finished in this pattern.
The second is that the backshift is not always required.
If the thing is still true, and you want the reader to know it is still true, you may leave it in the present.
She said the office is on the first floor, if it still is.
She said the office was on the first floor, which leaves the reader unsure whether it has moved.
In a record, that choice carries information, so it is worth making on purpose rather than by habit.

readings.title: Witness Statement: Incident on 11 March
readings.setting: A form completed after a workplace incident
readings.passage:
WITNESS STATEMENT
Name: D. Marchetti        Position: Shift supervisor
Incident date: 11 March        Statement taken: 13 March

1. At about 14:20 I noticed that the guard on the second press had been removed.
   It had been in place when I checked the line at 13:00.

2. I asked the operator whether he had removed it. He denied removing it.
   He stated that it had already been off when he took over at 14:00.

3. I instructed him to stop the press and I reported the matter to the duty manager.

4. The duty manager advised me not to restart the line until it had been inspected.
   She added that the inspection would take place the same afternoon.

5. I am recording paragraph 2 verbatim because the operator asked me to.
   His exact words were: 'It was off when I got here and I told Tom at two o'clock.'

In accordance with the site procedure, this statement is taken within 48 hours of the incident.
The line remains out of service pending the inspection report.
Signed: D. Marchetti

comprehension.q: What had the writer actually said at the meeting?
comprehension.a: That they could not confirm the date until the survey came back.
comprehension.why: Given in the second line, against what the minutes recorded.

comprehension.q: What exactly did the minute-writer do wrong, if they did not mishear?
comprehension.a: They paraphrased and dropped the condition.
comprehension.why: The text says paraphrasing is allowed and losing the condition is not.

comprehension.q: 'He mentioned the delay' became 'he complained about the delay'. What changed?
comprehension.a: A neutral reporting verb was replaced by one that judges the speaker.
comprehension.why: Mention is neutral; complain says the speaker was unhappy and makes them sound so.

comprehension.q: What does the writer now do, and why does it work?
comprehension.a: Asks for their own words to be recorded verbatim, and says so in the room.
comprehension.why: Verbatim words are the only thing that survives paraphrase.

comprehension.q: What does a past simple become when it is reported?
comprehension.why: I finished it becomes she said she had finished it.

comprehension.q: Why can the past perfect not step back?
comprehension.a: Because there is no tense further back for it to go to.
comprehension.why: The article says there is no such thing as had had finished in this pattern.

comprehension.q: Why does the article call the choice not to backshift informative?
comprehension.a: Leaving it in the present tells the reader it is still true.
comprehension.why: Was on the first floor leaves the reader unsure whether it has moved.

comprehension.q: When had the guard last been seen in place?
comprehension.a: At 13:00, when the supervisor checked the line.
comprehension.why: Paragraph 1, and the past perfect had been in place marks it as the earlier event.

comprehension.a: Because the operator asked for it to be.
comprehension.why: Stated in paragraph 5, with his exact words given.

comprehension.q: The statement says 'He denied removing it', not 'he denied to remove it'. Why?
comprehension.a: Deny takes an -ing form, never to plus a plain verb.
comprehension.why: It is one of the two verbs that break the person-plus-to shape.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Two past events, in the right order
speaking.instructions:
Join each pair aloud, putting the earlier event into the past perfect.
1. The meeting started at nine. I arrived at half past.
2. They closed at five. We rang at ten past.
3. She left her glasses at home. She could not sign it.
4. The parts were ordered. Then somebody checked the stock.
5. The guard was in place at one. At twenty past two it was gone.
A model for the first one:
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
Tap the mic. Say all five. Tap again and listen.
Check: in each one, is the EARLIER event the one with had?
Say number 1 again without had, and hear how the meaning changes.
speaking.tutor: Say your five and ask the tutor whether any pair came out in the wrong order.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The had you can barely hear
speaking.instructions:
In the past perfect, had is almost never stressed. It shrinks to a d.
That is why learners often do not hear it at all.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the stress.
I had finished        sounds like  I-d FINished
She had already left  sounds like  She-d alREADy left
They had closed       sounds like  They-d CLOSED
He said he had sent it  sounds like  He said he-d SENT it
The respelling is a hint for your ear. Always write had, or 'd.
Now say these three lines.
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
She said she had finished it the day before.
He denied removing it, and said it had already been off.
Tap the mic. Say the three lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: is had short and unstressed, joined to the word in front?
If you hear a strong HAD, say the line again faster.
speaking.tutor: Say the three lines and ask the tutor whether it could hear the had at all.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Report it a week later
speaking.instructions:
Report each one as if a week has passed. Step every tense back one.
1. 'I work here,' he said.
2. 'I am working on it now,' she said.
3. 'I finished it yesterday,' she said.
4. 'I have already sent it,' he said.
5. 'I will ring you tomorrow,' she said.
6. 'I can come on Friday,' he said.
7. 'I had already left,' she said.
Models: He said he worked there. She said she had finished it the day before.
Tap the mic. Report all seven. Tap again and listen.
Check: did the time words move as well as the tenses?
In number 7, did you leave it alone? It cannot step back any further.
speaking.tutor: Report the seven to the tutor and ask whether any time word stayed behind.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: the minutes that were wrong
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
What I said at the meeting was that I could not confirm the date until the survey came back.
What the minutes said was that I had refused to confirm the date.
Those are not the same thing, and by the time I saw them the paper had gone to the client.
The person who wrote them had not misheard me. They had paraphrased and lost the condition.
Every sentence I objected to had the same shape.
He mentioned the delay became he complained about the delay.
She said she would look into it became she reassured us it was in hand.
Nobody had lied, and the paper as a whole said something the meeting had not agreed.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. What had the speaker actually said?
2. What did the minutes say instead?
3. What had the writer of the minutes done wrong?
4. Give one example of a verb that was changed.
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 they could not confirm until the survey came back.
2 that they had refused. 3 paraphrased and dropped the condition.
4 mentioned became complained, or said became reassured.
speaking.tutor: Retell the problem in three sentences and ask which change was the most damaging.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Did it happen, or was it only meant to?
speaking.instructions:
Say each sentence aloud in the form that matches the fact given.
1. The door is unlocked. Say what you forgot.
2. You can picture yourself doing it. Say what you remember.
3. You nearly forgot but you did it. Say what you remembered.
4. You told him and you wish you had not. Say what you regret.
5. You moved it as an experiment. Say what you tried.
6. You attempted it and failed. Say what you tried.
Models: I forgot to lock it. I remember locking it.
Tap the mic. Say all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: numbers 5 and 6 use the same words and describe opposite outcomes.
Did yours come out differently from each other?
speaking.tutor: Say your six and ask the tutor to tell you, from the form alone, whether each thing happened.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: report an incident
speaking.instructions:
Describe an incident, real or invented, for two minutes, as if giving a statement.
Cover these four, in this order:
what you noticed, and what had happened before that
what you asked, and what you were told
what you were instructed or advised to do
what remains undecided
Use the past perfect at least three times, and at least three different reporting verbs.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: is every past perfect genuinely the earlier event?
Could you defend every reporting verb you used?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your statement and ask whether any reporting verb went beyond the facts.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Eight sentences with two past times
writing.prompt:
Write eight sentences about one incident, real or invented.
In each one, two things happened in the past and one came first.
Put the main story in the past simple and the earlier event in the past perfect.
One of the eight should be a plain sequence with NO past perfect, to show you know when not to use it.
writing.model:
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
By the time we rang, they had closed for the day.
She could not sign it because she had left her glasses at home.
The parts had been ordered before anybody checked the stock.
The guard had been in place when I checked the line at one.
He said it had already been off when he took over.
Nobody told the duty manager until the press had been stopped.
I got up, had breakfast and left. (a plain sequence: no perfect needed)
writing.criteria:
Seven sentences pair a past simple with a past perfect.
In every one, the past perfect marks the EARLIER event.
One sentence is a plain sequence, and is labelled as such.
No sentence uses the past perfect three times in a row.
writing.support: Write the two events of each sentence on separate lines first, with times beside them.
writing.extension: Take one sentence and remove the had. Write what it now claims instead.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Report a conversation a week later
writing.prompt:
Write out eight things that were said in a conversation, in quotation marks.
Then report each one as if a week has passed.
Include at least one present simple, one past simple, one present perfect,
one will, one can, and one past perfect.
writing.model:
'I work here.' -> He said he worked there.
'I am working on it now.' -> She said she was working on it then.
'I finished it yesterday.' -> She said she had finished it the day before.
'I have already sent it.' -> He said he had already sent it.
'I will ring you tomorrow.' -> She said she would ring me the next day.
'I can come on Friday.' -> He said he could come on Friday.
'I had already left.' -> She said she had already left.
'The office is on the first floor.' -> She said the office is on the first floor.
writing.criteria:
Every tense stepped back correctly.
The past perfect left unchanged, because it cannot step back.
Time and place words moved: here to there, yesterday to the day before.
One sentence deliberately NOT backshifted, with a note saying why.
writing.support: Write the tense of each original in the margin first. Then step it back one.
writing.extension: Take the one you did not backshift and write both versions. Say what each tells the reader.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A witness statement
writing.prompt:
Write a witness statement about an incident you invent, in the style of Reading 3.
Five numbered paragraphs. Include what you noticed, what had happened before,
what you asked, what you were told, and what you were instructed to do.
One paragraph must record somebody's exact words verbatim, and say why.
writing.model:
1. At about 14:20 I noticed that the guard on the second press had been removed.
   It had been in place when I checked the line at 13:00.
2. I asked the operator whether he had removed it. He denied removing it.
3. I instructed him to stop the press and reported the matter to the duty manager.
4. The duty manager advised me not to restart the line until it had been inspected.
5. I am recording paragraph 2 verbatim because the operator asked me to.
   His exact words were: 'It was off when I got here and I told Tom at two o'clock.'
writing.length: Five numbered paragraphs, about 120 to 160 words.
writing.criteria:
Past perfect used at least three times, each for a genuinely earlier event.
At least four different reporting verbs, all defensible.
One reported question, in statement order.
One verbatim quotation, with a reason given for recording it.
writing.support: Draw a timeline first, with the times down the left. The past perfect belongs to everything above the line you start at.
writing.extension: Write the one sentence in your statement that somebody could later dispute, and say how you would defend it.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Formal, then human
writing.prompt:
Write seven sentences using these formal phrases, one each:
in accordance with, with regard to, in the event of, subject to,
on behalf of, with a view to, pending.
Then rewrite any THREE of them as you would actually say them to a colleague,
and write one sentence on when the formal version is worth using.
writing.model:
Work was carried out in accordance with the specification.
With regard to your letter of the 3rd, I can confirm the date.
In the event of a power failure, the alarm sounds automatically.
Approval is subject to a final inspection.
I am writing on behalf of the residents of Priory Court.
We met with a view to agreeing a timescale.
The post is suspended pending the investigation.

About your letter, the date is fine.
If the power goes, the alarm goes off.
We met to try to agree a timescale.

The formal version is worth it where the document may be read by somebody
who was not there, or used in a dispute.
writing.starter: Work was carried out in accordance with …
writing.length: Seven sentences, three rewrites and one comment, about 110 to 150 words.
writing.criteria:
All seven phrases used correctly.
with a view to followed by an -ing form.
The three rewrites sound like speech, not like a shortened contract.
The final sentence names a situation, not a feeling.
writing.support: Write the plain meaning of each phrase beside it first, then build the formal sentence.
writing.extension: Find one formal phrase in a real document near you and write its plain version.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which happened first?
activities.instructions:
Choose the past simple or the past perfect.
1. When I ___ (arrive), the meeting ___ (already start).
2. By the time we ___ (ring), they ___ (close).
3. She ___ (not sign) it because she ___ (leave) her glasses at home.
4. I ___ (get) up, ___ (have) breakfast and ___ (leave).
5. The parts ___ (be) ordered before anybody ___ (check) the stock.
6. The guard ___ (be) in place when I ___ (check) the line at one.
Now say what each of these claims.
7. When I arrived, the meeting started.
8. When I arrived, the meeting had started.
activities.answers:
1. arrived / had already started  2. rang / had closed
3. did not sign / had left  4. got / had / left (a plain sequence)
5. had been ordered / checked  6. had been / checked
7. I arrived, and then it began.  8. It began, and then I came in late.
Number 4 is the one that needs NO past perfect, and knowing that is half the skill.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the two events of each sentence on separate lines with times beside them, then choose.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Step it back
activities.instructions:
Report each one as if a week has passed.
1. 'I work here,' he said.
2. 'I am working on it now,' she said.
3. 'I finished it yesterday,' she said.
4. 'I have already sent it,' he said.
5. 'I will ring you tomorrow,' she said.
6. 'I can come on Friday,' he said.
7. 'I had already left,' she said.
8. 'We are meeting here today,' they said.
Now correct this.
9. He said he had had finished it.
activities.answers:
1. He said he worked there.  2. She said she was working on it then.
3. She said she had finished it the day before.
4. He said he had already sent it.
5. She said she would ring me the next day.
6. He said he could come on Friday.
7. She said she had already left. (nowhere further to go)
8. They said they were meeting there that day.
9. He said he had finished it. The past perfect cannot step back twice.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the tense of each original in the margin before you touch it.

activities.title: Practice 3 — How much force?
activities.instructions:
Report each one with the verb that fits.
1. Your manager, with authority: 'Stop the line.'
2. A colleague, twice, with no authority: 'Get it in writing.'
3. An inspector, officially: 'Keep a written record.'
4. A friend: 'I think you should wait.'
5. A notice: 'No parking on the verge.'
6. A colleague: 'Why not wait until Friday?'
7. He said he had not sent the second invoice.
8. A manager, formally, in writing: 'Please supply a copy.'
Now correct these.
9. She suggested me to wait.
10. He denied to send it.
activities.answers:
1. ordered me to stop the line  2. urged me to get it in writing
3. instructed us to keep a written record  4. advised me to wait
5. forbids parking on the verge  6. suggested waiting until Friday
7. denied sending the second invoice  8. requested a copy
9. She suggested waiting. (or: that I wait)  10. He denied sending it.
suggest and deny are the two that break the person-plus-to shape.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, write down who had the power before you choose the verb.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Happened, or only intended?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form, and write what the sentence claims.
1. The door is unlocked. I forgot (locking / to lock) it.
2. I can picture doing it. I remember (locking / to lock) it.
3. I nearly forgot but I did it. I remembered (locking / to lock) it.
4. I told him and wish I had not. I regret (telling / to tell) him.
5. Bad news is coming. I regret (informing / to inform) you that ...
6. I moved it as an experiment. I tried (moving / to move) it.
7. I attempted it and failed. I tried (moving / to move) it.
8. I no longer eat there. I stopped (eating / to eat) there.
9. I halted in order to eat. I stopped (eating / to eat).
activities.answers:
1. to lock — it never happened  2. locking — it happened
3. to lock — the memory came first  4. telling — it happened
5. to inform — bad news coming  6. moving — it happened
7. to move — only attempted  8. eating — the habit ended
9. to eat — a halt for the purpose of eating
6 and 7 are the same words describing opposite outcomes; so are 8 and 9.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Beside each answer, write DID or MEANT. That is the whole distinction.

activities.title: Practice 5 — The formal phrase
activities.instructions:
Write the missing phrase.
1. Work was carried out ___ the specification. (following its rules)
2. ___ your letter of the 3rd, I can confirm the date. (about)
3. ___ a power failure, the alarm sounds. (if this happens)
4. Approval is ___ a final inspection. (only if satisfied)
5. I am writing ___ the residents. (as their representative)
6. We met ___ ___ agreeing a timescale. (in order eventually to)
7. The post is suspended ___ the investigation. (until decided)
8. ___ the works, the road is closed. (before)
Now correct these.
9. We met with a view to agree a timescale.
10. With regard to your email, I am in receipt of the same.
activities.answers:
1. in accordance with  2. With regard to  3. In the event of  4. subject to
5. on behalf of  6. with a view to  7. pending  8. Prior to
9. with a view to agreeING — the to there is a preposition, not an infinitive marker.
10. Thanks for your email. The original is correct English that nobody speaks.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the plain meaning beside each phrase first. If you cannot, you do not know it yet.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Put the condition back
activities.instructions:
Each line is a minute that lost something. Rewrite it so it records what was said.
The original words are given in brackets.
1. She refused to confirm the date.
   ('I cannot confirm the date until the survey comes back.')
2. He complained about the delay.
   ('There has been a delay on the second batch.')
3. She reassured us that it was in hand.
   ('I will look into it.')
4. He admitted the figures were wrong.
   ('These figures are from the earlier batch.')
5. They agreed to the timescale.
   ('We can meet that, provided the parts arrive by Friday.')
activities.answers:
1. She said she could not confirm the date until the survey came back.
2. He mentioned that there had been a delay on the second batch.
3. She said she would look into it.
4. He stated that the figures were from the earlier batch.
5. They said they could meet the timescale provided the parts arrived by Friday.
In 1 and 5 a CONDITION was dropped. In 2, 3 and 4 a neutral verb was replaced
by a loaded one. Both kinds of loss are common, and neither is a lie.
4 or 5 right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, write which was lost: a condition, or a neutral verb. Then rebuild it.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the statement
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. At what time was the guard last seen in place?
2. What did the operator say about when it came off?
3. Who advised against restarting the line?
4. Copy three past perfect verbs and say what each one is earlier than.
5. Copy the reported question and say how you know it is reported.
6. Why does the statement say 'denied removing' and not 'denied to remove'?
activities.answers:
1. 13:00, when the supervisor checked the line.
2. That it had already been off when he took over at 14:00.
3. The duty manager.
4. 'had been removed' (earlier than 14:20), 'had been in place' (earlier than the noticing),
   'had already been off' (earlier than his taking over), 'had been inspected' (before restarting).
5. 'I asked the operator whether he had removed it.' Statement order, whether, no question mark.
6. deny takes an -ing form and never to plus a plain verb.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Draw a timeline of the statement with times down the side before you answer.

quizzes.q: When I arrived, the meeting ___ already started.
quizzes.why: The starting came before the arriving, and the earlier of two past events takes had plus the past participle.

quizzes.q: 'When I arrived, the meeting started.' What does this claim?
options: It began, then I came in late.
I arrived, and then it began.
It began while I was arriving.
quizzes.a: I arrived, and then it began.
quizzes.why: Two past simples read in the order they are written. Only had started would put the meeting first.

quizzes.q: 'I finished it yesterday,' she said. Reported a week later:
options: She said she finished it yesterday.
She said she has finished it yesterday.
She said she had finished it the day before.
She said she had finished it yesterday.
quizzes.a: She said she had finished it the day before.
quizzes.why: A past simple steps back to a past perfect, and yesterday has to move too or a later reader will misdate it.

quizzes.q: 'I had already left,' she said. Reported:
options: She said she had had already left.
She said she has already left.
She said she had already left.
quizzes.a: She said she had already left.
quizzes.why: The past perfect cannot step back again. There is no tense further back for it to move to.

quizzes.q: A colleague with no authority says it twice: 'Get it in writing.' Report it.
options: She urged me to get it in writing.
She ordered me to get it in writing.
She instructed me to get it in writing.
She suggested me to get it in writing.
quizzes.a: She urged me to get it in writing.
quizzes.why: urged is strong and repeated but claims no authority. The last option is not English at all: suggest never takes person + to.
suggest takes an -ing form or a that clause, never a person followed by to. That I wait would also work.
deny takes an -ing form. refuse and decline take to, and object takes to plus a noun, so none of the other three fits.

quizzes.q: The door is unlocked. Which is true?
quizzes.why: to looks forward at an intention that was not carried out. The -ing versions all claim the locking actually happened.

quizzes.q: You moved it as an experiment, and it worked. Which is right?
quizzes.why: -ing is the real event: you did move it. tried TO move it would mean you attempted it and probably failed.
It means in order eventually to. The to in it is a preposition, which is why the verb takes -ing.

quizzes.q: The post is suspended ___ the investigation.
quizzes.why: pending means until a decision is made. prior to would say the suspension came before the investigation and then ended.

quizzes.q: A record says 'he complained about the delay'. He had said 'There has been a delay on the second batch.' What has changed?
options: Nothing; it is a fair paraphrase.
The batch number has been dropped.
A neutral remark has been made to sound like a grievance.
quizzes.a: A neutral remark has been made to sound like a grievance.
quizzes.why: He mentioned a fact. complained reports him as unhappy, which the original words do not support.

teacherNotes.note: This unit depends on Unit 7 and completes it. Unit 7 took 7Ug.10 and deliberately stopped short of the tense backshift, because the backshift needs the past perfect, which requires 8Ug.08 and could not be taught at Stage 7. A learner who skipped Unit 7 will meet the reporting verbs here without the fairness test that governs them.

The past perfect is taught nowhere below this unit. L2 U20 teaches the PRESENT perfect, which is a different form and a different job; learners who confuse the two usually do so because both contain a participle. Card 1 is the only fully new form in the unit.
Once learners meet the past perfect they overuse it, and every verb in a narrative acquires a had. Practice 1 item 4 is a plain sequence that needs none, and it is the item worth spending time on.
suggest + person + to is one of the most persistent errors at B1, because every neighbouring verb takes that shape. Teach suggest and deny together as a two-item exception list rather than as a rule.

In the remember/forget set, learners choose by which version sounds better, and both sound equally natural. The only reliable question is whether the thing happened. Practice 4 asks them to write DID or MEANT beside each answer for that reason.

Reading 1 and Practice 6 teach learners to audit a record against what was said. The lesson is explicitly that neither kind of loss — a dropped condition, or a loaded verb — requires anybody to have lied. Do not let the class read it as a story about dishonesty.

Writing 3, the witness statement, is where all five cards have to work at once: two past times, reported speech, a defensible reporting verb, a verbatim quotation and a formal phrase. It is the unit's real assessment.

selfAssessment.statement: I can use the past perfect for the earlier of two past events.
I know when a plain sequence needs no past perfect at all.
I can step the tenses back when I report something said last week.
I know the past perfect cannot step back any further.
I can choose between ordered, instructed, urged and advised.
I know that suggest and deny do not take a person plus to.
I can say whether I did something or only meant to.
I can read a formal phrase like subject to or pending without stopping.

assignment.title: The statement, and the record of it
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write a witness statement about an incident you invent, in five numbered
paragraphs and about 150 words. Use the past perfect at least four times, each for a
genuinely earlier event. Report at least one question, one instruction and one denial.
Record one thing verbatim and say why.
Part two. Now write the summary somebody ELSE produced from your statement, in about
sixty words, containing two faults: one dropped condition and one loaded reporting verb.
Part three. Write the email you would send asking for the summary to be corrected.
Name both faults, quote your own words, and say what the corrected version should read.
Use at least two formal preposition phrases in part one, and none at all in part three.
assignment.submissionType: A witness statement, a flawed summary and a correcting email
